title: No Squirrel at Rama's Bridge
source: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda 6(15) (Critical Edition; vulgate 6.22)

captions.instagram:
Did a little squirrel really help build Rama's bridge?

Almost everyone grew up with the little squirrel who carried sand to Rama's bridge. Valmiki's Ramayana tells the building differently: the Ocean himself rises, names Nala, son of Vishvakarma, as the builder and promises to hold the bridge up. The monkeys hurl trees and mountains into the sea. No squirrel, and no name written on the stones. The squirrel came later, in regional retellings like the Telugu Ranganatha Ramayanam.

Which version did you grow up with: the squirrel, the stones with Rama's name, or Nala's bridge? Tell us where you heard it 👇

captions.youtube_description:
Did a little squirrel really help build Rama's bridge?

Almost everyone grew up with the little squirrel who carried sand to Rama's bridge. Valmiki's Ramayana tells the building differently: the Ocean himself rises, names Nala, son of Vishvakarma, as the builder and promises to hold the bridge up. The monkeys hurl trees and mountains into the sea. No squirrel, and no name written on the stones. The squirrel came later, in regional retellings like the Telugu Ranganatha Ramayanam.

Which version did you grow up with: the squirrel, the stones with Rama's name, or Nala's bridge? Tell us where you heard it 👇

Source: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda 6(15) (Critical Edition; vulgate 6.22)
Verses:
• The Ocean (Sagara) himself rises from the sea and speaks to Rama with joined palms — 6.15.1-3
• The Ocean names Nala, son of Vishvakarma, as the builder and promises: 'I will hold it up' — 6.15.8-9
• Nala: he would not speak of his own merits unasked; let the bridge be built today — 6.15.13
• Monkeys in hundreds of thousands break trees (sala, mango, ashoka and more) and hurl mountains into the sea — 6.15.14-19
• Nala built the great bridge, ten yojanas wide and a hundred long; it shone like the path of Svati in the sky — 6.15.20-22
• All beings watched the wondrous bridge-building; the army crossed by Nala's bridge — 6.15.24, 6.15.31
• The Critical Edition chapter of the building (6.15, all 33 verses) has no squirrel and no name written on the stones — 6.15 (whole chapter)
• The squirrel story appears in later regional retellings; earliest known in the Telugu Ranganatha Ramayanam — secondary
• Opening śloka: “Nala built a great bridge, ten yojanas wide and a hundred yojanas long, in the middle of the ocean.” — 6.15.20
